overview: A once-dominant radiation of hoofed mammals represented today by horses, rhinoceroses and tapirs, together with a much richer extinct diversity.
evidenceSummary: The group is documented by abundant Eocene-to-Recent skeletons, teeth and occurrences; relationships among some early branches remain debated.

overview: Eocene browsers that evolved rapidly from modest-bodied ancestors into rhinoceros-sized forms with distinctive skull appendages.
traits: Paired nasal or frontal appendages in some genera
evidenceSummary: Abundant skulls and skeletons establish a rapid Eocene radiation, but their exact position near the base of Perissodactyla is not fully resolved.

overview: A European palaeothere related to the horse side of perissodactyl evolution, with several species adapted to forest browsing.
evidenceSummary: Teeth and skeletons are common in European Paleogene deposits; species boundaries and locomotor interpretations vary among studies.

overview: A hornless rhinocerotoid whose short limbs, broad torso, high-set eyes and river-deposit occurrences support a semi-aquatic interpretation.
evidenceSummary: Several traits and depositional settings are consistent with semi-aquatic habits, but that inference should not be generalized to all amynodonts.

overview: One of the largest known land-mammal lineages, comprising long-limbed, long-necked hornless rhinocerotoids of Oligocene Asia.
evidenceSummary: Skulls, jaws and postcranial remains support its rhinocerotoid identity; phylogenetic and dispersal hypotheses continue to be revised by new Asian fossils.

overview: A genus within the more diverse chalicothere radiation; this profile does not treat every family- or subfamily-level trait as diagnostic of Chalicotherium itself.
traits: Forelimb and feeding-posture interpretations require specimen-level attribution
evidenceSummary: Claw-bearing limbs are secure for chalicotheres, but this genus-level profile withholds family-wide branch-pulling and posture claims unless they are tied to identified Chalicotherium material.

overview: A widespread Miocene three-toed horse with low-crowned teeth suited primarily to browsing rather than dedicated grazing.
evidenceSummary: Dental crown height and wear support browsing, while occurrences document dispersal from North America into Eurasia.

regionalRanges.label: North American tribe-level range
regionalRanges.basis: The North American hipparionin radiation begins near 17 Ma and the classic four-genus synthesis extends to about 2 Ma; exact endpoints remain pending a revised genus-level synthesis.

regionalRanges.label: Old World first dispersal
regionalRanges.basis: The oldest well-supported Old World dispersal window is represented by early Hippotherium records in the Vienna Basin.

regionalRanges.label: Latest Old World regional records
regionalRanges.basis: Terminal records vary by lineage and region; the review places the latest Chinese and African hipparionins around or below 1 Ma rather than at the Holocene boundary.

overview: A tribe of tridactyl horses that diversified across the Old and New Worlds; this entity avoids treating the genus Hipparion sensu stricto as the entire radiation.
evidenceSummary: Abundant teeth and limb bones document wide ecological variation. Hipparionini is used here deliberately because historical broad use of Hipparion obscures distinct genera such as Cormohipparion and Neohipparion.

overview: A short-legged, barrel-bodied rhinoceros whose aquatic ecology is contested: Florida isotopes favor principally terrestrial populations, while multi-isotope evidence supports semi-aquatic T. major at Ashfall.

ecology.habitat: Open habitats, wetlands and river-adjacent plains; locality dependent
ecology.guild: Bulk grazer or wet-habitat mixed feeder

evidenceSummary: Body shape alone is insufficient to infer behavior. Florida and Ashfall isotope studies reach different ecological conclusions, so behavior is represented as species-, locality- and time-dependent.

overview: A cold-adapted Pleistocene rhinoceros of Eurasian steppe-tundra, known from skeletons, soft-tissue remains and prehistoric art.
evidenceSummary: Morphology supports cold adaptation and grazing. The display LAD is a global synthesis, distinct from regional fossil dates and from a 14.4 ka genomic sample that shows no obvious pre-extinction genomic erosion.
